title: StuBara roadmap
description: How this archive should grow over time.
content:
What StuBara should become

StuBara should grow into a personal research library rather than a pile of markdown files.

That means keeping the structure simple, but making the archive pleasant enough to revisit.

The first good shape

The most natural first structure is:
Research for long-form writing
Briefings for shorter recurring summaries
About for identity and framing

Writing rules
keep paragraphs readable on mobile
separate fact from interpretation
prefer clarity over grand wording
let short posts stay short

Design rules
soft but not childish
clean but not sterile
polished enough to feel branded
lightweight enough to maintain

The practical next steps
keep publishing a few real posts
refine the homepage only after content exists
make navigation feel natural
avoid overbuilding too early

The real goal

Not just to publish markdown.

To make a place that actually feels worth returning to.

title: The biggest bioscience industry shifts of the past year
description: A structured look at funding, China licensing, platform shifts, AI drug discovery, and cell & gene therapy resets.
content:
One-line thesis

Capital started moving again, but far more selectively — and the market became much harsher about what counts as scalable science.
China biotech became a core sourcing market

One of the clearest shifts over the past year is that global pharma increasingly treated China biotech as a serious early- and mid-stage sourcing market, not just a secondary pool of assets.

This matters because it changes where pipelines are filled, who captures early value, and how cross-border licensing now works in practice.
Bispecifics moved to the center of dealmaking

If earlier cycles were shaped by ADC enthusiasm, the recent period has made bispecific and multispecific assets feel much more central to licensing and portfolio strategy.

The point is not just novelty. The point is that platform design itself is becoming part of the value proposition.
AI drug discovery shifted from theme to contract structure

AI is still not the same thing as validated clinical success. But it is no longer just presentation material either.

The industry increasingly uses AI as part of real discovery partnerships, workflow efficiency, and platform valuation logic.
Cell and gene therapy entered a reset phase

The science still matters. But the market now asks harder questions about manufacturing complexity, delivery, safety, access, and economic scalability.

That is why newer interest has tilted toward in vivo delivery, LNP-based systems, and approaches that reduce operational friction.
Funding became more selective, not broadly healthy

The market did not fully thaw. Instead, it became more polarised.

Strong assets still attracted attention. Weak or ambiguous stories found it much harder to raise capital, sustain valuations, or justify broad pipelines.
Commercial reality matters more than platform excitement

Approval still matters, but commercial viability matters more than before:
launch quality
reimbursement logic
manufacturing reliability
real patient access
actual revenue scaling

Final view

The strongest way to read the last year is this:
innovation supply shifted eastward
dealmaking favored better engineered platforms
AI became more operationally real
cell and gene therapy faced a harder commercial test
capital rewarded fewer winners

In other words, the industry moved one step further away from pure scientific excitement and closer to industrial discipline.
